docs.title: go-richdoc
docs.text:
One rich-document model, and the converters that read and write it — Markdown, LaTeX, reStructuredText, HTML, EPUB, Kindle MOBI, FictionBook, email, CSV, JSON, XML and plain text.

Part of the Documents, typesetting & fonts family of the pure-Go ecosystem — 10 modules, all CGO_ENABLED=0.

docs.title: What is here
docs.text:
This site is the organisation's reference index: what each module is, and where its API documentation lives. The API itself is generated from the source and served by pkg.go.dev, which is always current with the released tags — duplicating it here would only create a second copy to go stale.

  • Modules — every module in go-richdoc, with its source and its reference.

docs.title: One thing to know before converting untrusted input
docs.text:
A converter turns one format into another, so the question is whether CONTENT CAN BECOME MARKUP on the way out. It could, once: a Markdown heading of # <b>.. include:: /etc/passwd</b> became a reST directive, because reST tries explicit markup before it tries a title — and a docutils parse with a source path then reads that file. Fixed in rst v0.3.0, with a probe over every position a document can hold text to say it was the only one (injectprobe: 14 pairs where text became markup, 0 after; nothing at all in markdown or latex).

What no converter here protects you from, because the reference does not either: a URI scheme. javascript:alert(1) in a link survives every hop, and docutils writes the same href. An allow-list belongs in whatever renders the model. Each repository's README has a Security section with its own audit.

docs.title: The model, in one paragraph
docs.text: richdoc is a typed tree: a Document of Blocks and Inlines, both CLOSED interface sets, so a converter can type-switch over them exhaustively. Each converter maps one format onto that tree in both directions. Where a format has something the model does not, the converter says so in its own README with the population it measured — that is how the model grows: Classes on the nodes that carry them (v0.4.0), Cell.Blocks and Table.Caption (v0.5.0), each added because a corpus showed what was being dropped, and each additive so no existing consumer breaks.

docs.title: What every module here is held to
docs.text:
• CGO_ENABLED=0: no cgo, and no shelling out to a command-line tool in place of a library.

  • Built for ten targets — linux/{amd64,arm64,riscv64,loong64,ppc64le,s390x}, darwin/{amd64,arm64}, windows/amd64 and js/wasm — and tested on amd64, with the race detector.

    ⛔ Built is not tested, and this page used to say both at once

    It read "built and tested on amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le and s390x". Cross-compiling proves a program compiles; it says nothing about what it does when a byte order or a word size differs. These modules are a tree and a great deal of string handling, which is a different risk from a format whose integers come off a disk — and where that is the risk, the lane exists: go-ooxml runs its suite under qemu on five more architectures, big-endian s390x included, because an OPC package is a ZIP full of little-endian integers.

    • 100% statement coverage as a CI gate, error branches included — with one stated exception: rst enforces a 94% floor instead. It walks a doctree whose exact shape it does not control (go-docutils/docutils is a separate, independently evolving engine), so its ok-checked type assertions and its default: case for an unknown doctree tag are a safety net for a FUTURE tag rather than dead code. The reason is in that repository's own workflow, beside the number.
    • BSD-3-Clause.

The standard is described in full on the ecosystem map.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
The 10 modules of go-richdoc. Each links to its source and to its generated API reference.

Module What it is Directions Reference richdoc the model itself: the tree, and Walk, Clone, PlainText and a builder — pkg.go.dev markdown CommonMark + GFM tables and strikethrough, delegating the parse to goldmark read, write pkg.go.dev latex a practical subset of LaTeX, plus a PDF subpackage read, write pkg.go.dev rst reStructuredText, delegating the parse to go-docutils/docutils read, write pkg.go.dev data CSV, JSON, XML and plain text, plus the richdata command read pkg.go.dev fb2 FictionBook 2 (.fb2): one XML file, images base64 inside it read pkg.go.dev html HTML and XHTML, delegating the parse to golang.org/x/net/html read pkg.go.dev epub EPUB 2 and 3: the ZIP, the manifest and the spine, chapters through html read pkg.go.dev email RFC 5322 messages and MIME, HTML parts through html read pkg.go.dev mobi Kindle MOBI: a Palm database, a PalmDOC stream and one HTML document, through html read pkg.go.dev

Which directions a module has is in the table, because "converter" said of a one-way reader is the kind of claim that costs somebody an afternoon. A module that only reads is not unfinished: a .fb2, an EPUB, a mailbox or a .csv is a source, and writing one back is a job nobody has asked for.

docs.title: ⛔ One missing reader was three missing formats
docs.text: html is not a format anybody asked this organisation for. It is the piece epub and email both needed — EPUB's content documents are XHTML and an HTML mail's body is HTML — and mobi needed it as well: a MOBI's text IS one HTML document, cut into 4096-byte pieces and each piece compressed on its own. Three entries on go-pdfkit's parity table were blocked on one reader, which is the argument for naming a gap rather than working around it: all three are closed now, and the third is mobi.

docs.title: ⛔ And the shared reader is where the next defect was
docs.text:
Reading a real Kindle book is also what found go-richdoc/html#4: a space following an inline element is dropped, so <i>Walt Whitman</i> has comes out as one word. It had been there all along, under epub and email too — any paragraph with an <i>, a <b>, a <span> or a link loses a space at every one of those boundaries.

What made it visible was a second rendering of the same text: Project Gutenberg publishes a MOBI and a plain text of every title it has, and 125 816 words against 126 630 is a question a reader cannot ask of its own output. A shared reader multiplies a defect by its callers, which is the same property that made it worth writing once.

A one-line summary each, and nothing more: what a converter does with a construct its format cannot express lives in that repository's README, beside the measurement that decided it, so there is one place to correct when it changes.
